entries.827ccfc33021e65a1edac83a6bb65e63731714f9: <div sID="gen31489" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="2Cor.5" sID="2Cor.5"/> <div eID="gen31489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31490" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31491" type="x-p"/> The apostle proceeds in showing the reasons why they did not faint under their afflictions, namely, their expectation, desire, and assurance of happiness after death (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1-2Cor.5.5">ver. 1-5</reference>), and deduces an inference for the comfort of believers in their present state (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.6-2Cor.5.8">ver. 6-8</reference>), and another to quicken them in their duty, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.9-2Cor.5.11">ver. 9-11</reference>. Then he makes an apology for seeming to commend himself, and gives a good reason for his zeal and diligence (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.12-2Cor.5.15">ver. 12-15</reference>), and mentions two things that are necessary in order to our living to Christ, regeneration and reconciliation, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.16-2Cor.5.21">ver. 16, to the end</reference>.
entries.08e2b606788d976e2c66779ccc43795b712d21c0: <div eID="gen31491" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31490" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Believer's Prospect beyond Death. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31492" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> For we know that if our earthly house of <hi type="italic">this</hi> tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. <hi type="super">2</hi> For in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven: <hi type="super">3</hi> If so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked. <hi type="super">4</hi> For we that are in <hi type="italic">this</hi> tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life. <hi type="super">5</hi> Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing <hi type="italic">is</hi> God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit. <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore <hi type="italic">we are</hi> always confident, knowing that, whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord: <hi type="super">7</hi> (For we walk by faith, not by sight:) <hi type="super">8</hi> We are confident, <hi type="italic">I say,</hi> and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord. <hi type="super">9</hi> Wherefore we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him. 10 For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things <hi type="italic">done</hi> in <hi type="italic">his</hi> body, according to that he hath done, whether <hi type="italic">it be</hi> good or bad. <hi type="super">11</hi> Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences. <div eID="gen31492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31493" type="x-p"/> The apostle in these verses pursues the argument of the former chapter, concerning the grounds of their courage and patience under afflictions. And, <div eID="gen31493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31494" type="x-p"/> I. He mentions their expectation, and desire, and assurance, of eternal happiness after death, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1-2Cor.5.5">v. 1-5</reference>. Observe particularly, <div eID="gen31494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31495" type="x-p"/> 1. The believer's expectation of eternal happiness after death, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">v. 1</reference>. He does not only know, or is well assured by faith of the truth and reality of the thing itself—that there is another and a happy life after this present life is ended, but he has good hope through grace of his interest in that everlasting blessedness of the unseen world: "We know that we have a building of God, we have a firm and well-grounded expectation of the future felicity." Let us take notice, (1.) What heaven is in the eye and hope of a believer. He looks upon it as a house, or habitation, a dwelling-place, a resting-place, a hiding-place, our Father's house, where there are many mansions, and our everlasting home. It is a house in the heavens, in that high and holy place which as far excels all the palaces of this earth as the heavens are high above the earth. It is a building of God, whose builder and maker is God, and therefore is worthy of its author; the happiness of the future state is what God hath prepared for those that love him. It is eternal in the heavens, everlasting habitations, not like the earthly tabernacles, the poor cottages of clay in which our souls now dwell, which are mouldering and decaying, and <hi type="italic">whose foundations are in the dust.</hi> (2.) When it is expected this happiness shall be enjoyed—immediately after death, so soon as <hi type="italic">our house of this earthly tabernacle is dissolved.</hi> Note, [1.] That the body, this earthly house, is but a tabernacle, that must be dissolved shortly; the nails or pins will be drawn, and the cords be loosed, and then the body will return to dust as it was. [2.] When this comes to pass, then comes the house not made with hands. The spirit returns to God who gave it; and such as have walked with God here shall dwell with God for ever. <div eID="gen31495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31496" type="x-p"/> 2. The believer's earnest desire after this future blessedness, which is expressed by this word, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">stenazomen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">we groan,</hi> which denotes, (1.) A groaning of sorrow under a heavy load; so believers groan under the burden of life: <hi type="italic">In this we groan earnestly,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.2">v. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">We that are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.4">v. 4</reference>. The body of flesh is a heavy burden, the calamities of life are a heavy load. But believers groan because burdened with a body of sin, and the many corruptions that are still remaining and raging in them. This makes them complain, <hi type="italic">O wretched man that I am!</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.7.24">Rom. vii. 24</reference>. (2.) There is a groaning of desire after the happiness of another life; and thus believers groan: <hi type="italic">Earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.2">v. 2</reference>), to obtain a blessed immortality, <hi type="italic">that mortality might be swallowed up of life</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">that being found clothed, we may not be naked</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.3">v. 3</reference>), that, if it were the will of God, we might not sleep, but be changed; for it is not desirable in itself to be unclothed. Death considered merely as a separation of soul and body is not to be desired, but rather dreaded; but, considered as a passage to glory, the believer is <hi type="italic">willing rather</hi> to die than live, <hi type="italic">to be absent from the body, that he may be present with the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">v. 1</reference>), to leave this body that he may go to Christ, and to put off these rags of mortality that he may put on the robes of glory. Note, [1.] Death will strip us of the clothing of flesh, and all the comforts of life, as well as put an end to all our troubles here below. Naked we came into this world, and naked shall we go out of it. But, [2.] Gracious souls are not found naked in the other world; no, they are clothed with garments of praise, with robes of righteousness and glory. They shall be delivered out of all their troubles, and shall have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.14">Rev. vii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen31496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31497" type="x-p"/> 3. The believer's assurance of his interest in this future blessedness, on a double account:—(1.) From the experience of the grace of God, in preparing and making him meet for this blessedness. He that hath <hi type="italic">wrought us for the self-same thing is God,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.5">v. 5</reference>. Note, All who are designed for heaven hereafter are wrought or prepared for heaven while they are here; the stones of that spiritual building and temple above are squared and fashioned here below. And he that hath wrought us for this is God, because nothing less than a divine power can make a soul partaker of a divine nature; no hand less than the hand of God can work us for this thing. A great deal is to be done to prepare our souls for heaven, and that preparation of the heart is from the Lord. (2.) The <hi type="italic">earnest of the Spirit</hi> gave them this assurance: for an earnest is part of payment, and secures the full payment. The present graces and comforts of the Spirit are earnests of everlasting grace and comfort. <div eID="gen31497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31498" type="x-p"/> II. The apostle deduces an inference for the comfort of believers in their present state and condition in this world, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.6-2Cor.5.8">v. 6-8</reference>. Here observe, 1. What their present state or condition is: they <hi type="italic">are absent from the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.6">v. 6</reference>); they are pilgrims and strangers in this world; they do but sojourn here in their earthly home, or in this tabernacle; and though God is with us here, by his Spirit, and in his ordinances, yet we are not with him as we hope to be: we cannot see his face while we live: <hi type="italic">For we walk by faith, not by sight,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.7">v. 7</reference>. We have not the vision and fruition of God, as of an object that is present with us, and as we hope for hereafter, when we <hi type="italic">shall see as we are seen.</hi> Note, Faith is for this world, and sight is reserved for the other world: and it is our duty, and will be our interest, to walk by faith, till we come to live by sight. 2. How comfortable and courageous we ought to be in all the troubles of life, and in the hour of death: <hi type="italic">Therefore we are,</hi> or ought to be, <hi type="italic">always confident</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.6">v. 6</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">We are confident, and willing rather to be absent from the body.</hi> True Christians, if they duly considered the prospect faith gives them of another world, and the good reasons of their hope of blessedness after death, would be comforted under the troubles of life, and supported in the hour of death: they should take courage, when they are encountering the last enemy, and be willing rather to die than live, when it is the will of God that they should <hi type="italic">put off this tabernacle.</hi> Note, As those who are born from above long to be there, so it is but being absent from the body, and we shall very soon be present with the Lord—but to die, and be with Christ—but to close our eyes to all things in this world, and we shall open them in a world of glory. Faith will be turned into sight. <div eID="gen31498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31499" type="x-p"/> III. He proceeds to deduce an inference to excite and quicken himself and others to duty, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.9-2Cor.5.11">v. 9-11</reference>. So it is that well-grounded hopes of heaven will be far from giving the least encouragement to sloth and sinful security; on the contrary, they should stir us up to use the greatest care and diligence in religion: <hi type="italic">Wherefore,</hi> or because we hope to be present with the Lord, <hi type="italic">we labour</hi> and take pains, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.9">v. 9</reference>. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Philotimoumetha</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">We are ambitious,</hi> and labour as industriously as the most ambitious men do to obtain what they aim at. Here observe, 1. What it was that the apostle was thus ambitious of—<hi type="italic">acceptance with God.</hi> We labour that, living and dying, whether present in the body or absent from the body, <hi type="italic">we may be accepted of him,</hi> the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.9">v. 9</reference>), that we <hi type="italic">may please him who hath chosen us,</hi> that our great Lord may say to us, <hi type="italic">Well done.</hi> This they coveted as the greatest favour and the highest honour: it was the summit of their ambition. 2. What further quickening motives they had to excite their diligence, from the consideration of the judgment to come, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10-2Cor.5.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. There are many things relating to this great matter that should awe the best of men into the utmost care and diligence in religion; for example, the certainty of this judgment, for we must appear; the universality of it, for we must all appear; the great Judge before whose judgment-seat we must appear, the Lord Jesus Christ, who himself will appear in flaming fire; the recompence to be then received, for things done in the body, which will be very particular (unto every one), and very just, according to what we have done, whether good or bad. The apostle calls this awful judgment <hi type="italic">the terror of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.11">v. 11</reference>), and, by the consideration thereof, was excited to persuade men to repent, and live a holy life, that, when Christ shall appear terribly, they may appear before him comfortably. And, concerning his fidelity and diligence, he comfortably appeals unto God, and the consciences of those he wrote to: <hi type="italic">We are made manifest unto God, and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences.</hi>
entries.5a555c71fdbcd277e0048a0d2fa7a8d16b967ef5: <div eID="gen31499" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Apology for Seeming Self-Commendation. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31500" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> For we commend not ourselves again unto you, but give you occasion to glory on our behalf, that ye may have somewhat to <hi type="italic">answer</hi> them which glory in appearance, and not in heart. <hi type="super">13</hi> For whether we be beside ourselves, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> to God: or whether we be sober, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> for your cause. 14 For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead: <hi type="super">15</hi> And <hi type="italic">that</hi> he died for all, that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again. <div eID="gen31500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31501" type="x-p"/> Here observe, I. The apostle makes an apology for seeming to commend himself and his fellow-labourers (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.13">v. 13</reference>), and tells them, 1. It was not to commend themselves, nor for their own sakes, that he had spoken of their fidelity and diligence in the <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1-2Cor.5.11">former verses</reference>; nor was he willing to suspect their good opinion of him. But, 2. The true reason was this, to put an argument in their mouths wherewith to answer his accusers, who made vain boastings, and gloried in appearances only; that he might give them <hi type="italic">an occasion to glory on their behalf,</hi> or to defend them against the reproaches of their adversaries. And if the people can say that the word has been manifested to their consciences, and been effectual to their conversion and edification, this is the best defence they can make for the ministry of the word, when they are vilified and reproached. <div eID="gen31501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31502" type="x-p"/> II. He gives good reasons for their great zeal and diligence. Some of Paul's adversaries had, it is likely, reproached him for his zeal and fervour, as if he had been a madman, or, in the language of our days, a fanatic; they imputed all to enthusiasm, as the Roman governor told him, <hi type="italic">Much learning has made thee mad,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.26.24">Acts xxvi. 24</reference>. But the apostle tells them, 1. It was for the glory of God, and the good of the church, that he was thus zealous and industrious: "<hi type="italic">Whether we be beside ourselves, or whether we be sober</hi> (whether you or others do think the one or the other), it is <hi type="italic">to God,</hi> and for his glory: and it is <hi type="italic">for your cause,</hi> or to promote your good," <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.13">v. 13</reference>. If they manifested the greatest ardour and vehemency at some times, and used the greatest calmness in strong reasonings at other times, it was for the best ends; and in both methods they had good reason for what they did. For, 2. <hi type="italic">The love of Christ constrained them,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.14">v. 14</reference>. They were under the sweetest and strongest constraints to do what they did. Love has a constraining virtue to excite ministers and private Christians in their duty. Our love to Christ will have this virtue; and Christ's love to us, which was manifested in this great instance of his dying for us, will have this effect upon us, if it be duly considered and rightly judged of. For observe how the apostle argues for the reasonableness of love's constraints, and declares, (1.) What we were before, and must have continued to be, had not Christ died for us: <hi type="italic">We were dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.14">v. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">If one died for all, then were all dead;</hi> dead in law, under sentence of death; dead in sins and trespasses, spiritually dead. Note, This was the deplorable condition of all those for whom Christ died: they were lost and undone, dead and ruined, and must have remained thus miserable for ever if Christ had not died for them. (2.) What such should do, for whom Christ died; namely, that they should live to him. This is what Christ designed, that <hi type="italic">those who live,</hi> who are made alive unto God by means of his death, <hi type="italic">should live to him that died for them, and rose again</hi> for their sakes also, and that they should not live <hi type="italic">to themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.15">v. 15</reference>. Note, We should not make ourselves, but Christ, the end of our living and actions: and it was one end of Christ's death to cure us of this self-love, and to excite us always to act under the commanding influence of his love. A Christian's life should be consecrated to Christ; and then do we live as we ought to live when we live to Christ, who died for us.
entries.a26c7ec02da790c262e9c73a26b99e130231eaef: <div eID="gen31502" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ministry of the Apostles. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31503" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh: yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we <hi type="italic">him</hi> no more. <hi type="super">17</hi> Therefore if any man <hi type="italic">be</hi> in Christ, <hi type="italic">he is</hi> a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. <hi type="super">18</hi> And all things <hi type="italic">are</hi> of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation; 19 To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation. <hi type="super">20</hi> Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech <hi type="italic">you</hi> by us: we pray <hi type="italic">you</hi> in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God. 21 For he hath made him <hi type="italic">to be</hi> sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. <div eID="gen31503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31504" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle mentions two things that are necessary in order to our living to Christ, both of which are the consequences of Christ's dying for us; namely, regeneration and reconciliation. <div eID="gen31504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31505" type="x-p"/> I. Regeneration, which consists of two things; namely, 1. Weanedness from the world: "<hi type="italic">Henceforth we know no man after the flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.16">v. 16</reference>. We do not own nor affect any person or thing in this world for carnal ends and outward advantage: we are enabled, by divine grace, not to mind nor regard this world, nor the things of this world, but to live above it. The love of Christ is in our hearts, and the world is under our feet." Note, Good Christians must enjoy the comforts of this life, and their relations in this world, with a holy indifference. <hi type="italic">Yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet,</hi> says the apostle, <hi type="italic">we know him no more.</hi> It is questioned whether Paul had seen Christ in the flesh. However, the rest of the apostles had, and so might some among those he was now writing to. However, he would not have them value themselves upon that account; for even the bodily presence of Christ is not to be desired nor doted upon by his disciples. We must live upon his spiritual presence, and the comfort it affords. Note, Those who make images of Christ, and use them in their worship, do not take the way that God has appointed for strengthening their faith and quickening their affections; for it is the will of God that we should not know Christ any more after the flesh. 2. A thorough change of the heart: <hi type="italic">For if any man be in Christ,</hi> if any man be a Christian indeed, and will approve himself such, <hi type="italic">he is,</hi> or he must be, <hi type="italic">a new creature,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.17">v. 17</reference>. Some read it, <hi type="italic">Let him be a new creature.</hi> This ought to be the care of all who profess the Christian faith, that they be new creatures; not only that they have a new name, and wear a new livery, but that they have a new heart and new nature. And so great is the change the grace of God makes in the soul, that, as it follows, <hi type="italic">old things are passed away</hi>—old thoughts, old principles, and old practices, are passed away; and <hi type="italic">all these things must become new.</hi> Note, Regenerating grace creates a new world in the soul; all things are new. The renewed man acts from new principles, by new rules, with new ends, and in new company. <div eID="gen31505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31506" type="x-p"/> II. Reconciliation, which is here spoken of under a double notion:— <div eID="gen31506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31507" type="x-p"/> 1. As an unquestionable privilege, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18-2Cor.5.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. Reconciliation supposes a quarrel, or breach of friendship; and sin has made a breach, it has broken the friendship between God and man. The heart of the sinner is filled with enmity against God, and God is justly offended with the sinner. Yet, behold, there may be a reconciliation; the offended Majesty of heaven is willing to be reconciled. And observe, 1. He has appointed the Mediator of reconciliation. He has reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18">v. 18</reference>. God is to be owned from first to last in the undertaking and performance of the Mediator. All things relating to our reconciliation by Jesus Christ are of God, who by the mediation of Jesus Christ has reconciled the world to himself, and put himself into a capacity of being actually reconciled to offenders, without any wrong or injury to his justice or holiness, and does not impute to men their trespasses, but recedes from the rigour of the first covenant, which was broken, and does not insist upon the advantage he might justly take against us for the breach of that covenant, but is willing to enter into a new treaty, and into a new covenant of grace, and, according to the tenour thereof, freely to forgive us all our sins, and justify freely by his grace all those who do believe. 2. He has appointed the <hi type="italic">ministry of reconciliation,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18">v. 18</reference>. By the inspiration of God the scriptures were written, which contain the word of reconciliation, showing us that peace was made by the blood of the cross, that reconciliation is wrought, and directing us how we may be interested therein. And he has appointed the office of the ministry, which is a <hi type="italic">ministry of reconciliation:</hi> ministers are to open and proclaim to sinners the terms of mercy and reconciliation, and persuade them to comply therewith. For, <div eID="gen31507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31508" type="x-p"/> 2. Reconciliation is here spoken of as our indispensable duty, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.20">v. 20</reference>. As God is willing to be reconciled to us, we ought to be reconciled to God. And it is the great end and design of the gospel, that word of reconciliation, to prevail upon sinners to lay aside their enmity against God. Faithful ministers are Christ's ambassadors, sent to treat with sinners on peace and reconciliation: they come in God's name, with his entreaties, and act in Christ's stead, doing the very thing he did when he was upon this earth, and what he wills to be done now that he is in heaven. Wonderful condescension! Though God can be no loser by the quarrel, nor gainer by the peace, yet by his ministers he beseeches sinners to lay aside their enmity, and accept of the terms he offers, that they would be reconciled to him, to all his attributes, to all his laws, and to all his providences, to believe in the Mediator, to accept the atonement, and comply with his gospel, in all the parts of it and in the whole design of it. And for our encouragement so to do the apostle subjoins what should be well known and duly considered by us (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">v. 21</reference>), namely, (1.) The purity of the Mediator: <hi type="italic">He knew no sin.</hi> (2.) The sacrifice he offered: <hi type="italic">He was made sin;</hi> not a sinner, but <hi type="italic">sin,</hi> that is, a sin-offering, a sacrifice for sin. (3.) The end and design of all this: that <hi type="italic">we might be made the righteousness of God in him,</hi> might be justified freely by the grace of God through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus. Note, [1.] As Christ, who knew no sin of his own, was made sin for us, so we, who have no righteousness of our own, are made the righteousness of God in him. [2.] Our reconciliation to God is only through Jesus Christ, and for the sake of his merit: on him therefore we must rely, and make mention of his righteousness and his only.  <chapter eID="2Cor.5"/> <div eID="gen31508" type="x-p"/>

entries.b1e02de7ff591a25e204ed12a9832c9b051b5a56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17245"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <div sID="gen34275" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1-2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:1-21</reference>. The Hope (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">2Co 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.18">18</reference>) OF Eternal Glory in the Resurrection Body.<div eID="gen34275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34276" type="x-p"/> Hence arises his ambition to be accepted at the Lord's coming judgment. Hence, too, his endeavor to deal openly with men, as with God, in preaching; thus giving the Corinthians whereof to boast concerning him against his adversaries. His constraining motive is the transforming love of Christ, by whom God has wrought reconciliation between Himself and men, and has committed to the apostle the ministry of reconciliation.<div eID="gen34276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34277" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17245"/><hi type="bold">1. For--</hi>Assigning the reason for the statement (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">2Co 4:17</reference>), that affliction leads to exceeding glory.<div eID="gen34277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we know--</hi>assuredly (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.14">2Co 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>).<div eID="gen34278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34279" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if--</hi>For all shall not die; many shall be "changed" without "dissolution" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51-1Cor.15.53">1Co 15:51-53</reference>). If this daily delivering unto death (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.11">2Co 3:11</reference>) should end in actual death.<div eID="gen34279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earthly--</hi>not the same as earthy (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.47">1Co 15:47</reference>). It stands in contrast to "in the heavens."<div eID="gen34280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34281" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house of this tabernacle--</hi>rather, "house of the tabernacle." "House" expresses more permanency than belongs to the body; therefore the qualification, "of the tabernacle" (implying that it is shifting, not stationary), is added (compare <reference osisRef="Job.4.19">Job 4:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.13">2Pe 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>). It thus answers to the tabernacle in the wilderness. Its wooden frame and curtains wore out in course of time when Israel dwelt in Canaan, and a fixed temple was substituted for it. The temple and the tabernacle in all essentials were one; there was the same ark, the same cloud of glory. Such is the relation between the "earthly" body and the resurrection body. The Holy Spirit is enshrined in the believer's body as in a sanctuary (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.16">1Co 3:16</reference>). As the ark went first in taking down the wilderness tabernacle, so the soul (which like the ark is sprinkled with blood of atonement, and is the sacred deposit in the inmost shrine, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2Ti 1:12</reference>) in the dissolution of the body; next the coverings were removed, answering to the flesh; lastly, the framework and boards, answering to the bones, which are last to give way (<reference osisRef="Num.4.1-Num.4.49">Nu 4:1-49</reference>). Paul, as a tent-maker, uses an image taken from his trade (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.3">Ac 18:3</reference>).<div eID="gen34281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34282" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dissolved--</hi>a mild word for death, in the case of believers.<div eID="gen34282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we have--</hi>in assured prospect of possession, as certain as if it were in our hands, laid up "in the heavens" for us. The tense is present (compare <reference osisRef="John.3.36">Joh 3:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.47">6:47</reference>, "hath").<div eID="gen34283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34284" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a building of God--</hi>rather "from God." A solid building, not a temporary tabernacle or tent. "Our" body stands in contrast to "from God." For though our present body be also from God, yet it is not fresh and perfect from His hands, as our resurrection body shall be.<div eID="gen34284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34285" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not made with hands--</hi>contrasted with houses erected by man's hands (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.44-1Cor.15.49">1Co 15:44-49</reference>). So Christ's body is designated, as contrasted with the tabernacle reared by Moses (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.58">Mr 14:58</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11">He 9:11</reference>). This "house" can only be the resurrection body, in contrast to the "earthly house of the tabernacle," our present body. The intermediate state is not directly taken into account. A comma should separate "eternal," and "in the heavens." <div eID="gen34285" type="x-p"/>
entries.55c479d54943e214e4d8688e6338f9f32348f633: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17246"/><div sID="gen34286" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17246"/><hi type="bold">2. For in this--</hi>Greek, "For also in this"; "herein" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.10">2Co 8:10</reference>). Alford takes it, "in this" tabernacle. <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.4">2Co 5:4</reference>, which seems parallel, favors this. But the parallelism is sufficiently exact by making "in this we groan" refer generally to what was just said (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2Co 5:1</reference>), namely, that we cannot obtain our "house in the heavens" except our "earthly tabernacle" be first dissolved by death.<div eID="gen34286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we groan--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.8.23">Ro 8:23</reference>) under the body's weaknesses now and liability to death.<div eID="gen34287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34288" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earnestly desiring to be clothed upon--</hi>translate, "earnestly longing to have ourselves clothed upon," &c., namely, by being found alive at Christ's coming, and so to escape dissolution by death (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2Co 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.4">4</reference>), and to have our heavenly body put on over the earthly. The groans of the saints prove the existence of the longing desire for the heavenly glory, a desire which cannot be planted by God within us in vain, as doomed to disappointment.<div eID="gen34288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34289" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our house--</hi>different Greek from that in <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2Co 5:1</reference>; translate, "our habitation," "our domicile"; it has a more distinct reference to the inhabitant than the general term "house" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2Co 5:1</reference>) [Bengel].<div eID="gen34289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34290" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from heaven--</hi>This domicile is "from heaven" in its origin, and is to be brought to us by the Lord at His coming again "from heaven" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">1Th 4:16</reference>). Therefore this "habitation" or "domicile" is not heaven itself. <div eID="gen34290" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa61879a9b47ee52ea77c48ef6afacc64e485be8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17247"/><div sID="gen34291" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17247"/><hi type="bold">3. If so be, &c.--</hi>Our "desire" holds good, should the Lord's coming find us alive. Translate, "If so be that having ourselves clothed (with our natural body, compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.4">2Co 5:4</reference>) we shall not be found naked (stripped of our present body)." <div eID="gen34291" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d0db97fcb2281dd9d9e4bc2c30694167873861e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17248"/><div sID="gen34292" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17248"/><hi type="bold">4. For--</hi>resuming <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.2">2Co 5:2</reference>.<div eID="gen34292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being burdened: not for that--</hi>rather, "in that we desire not to have ourselves unclothed (of our present body), but clothed upon (with our heavenly body).<div eID="gen34293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that mortality, &c.--</hi>rather, "that what is mortal (our mortal part) may be swallowed up of (absorbed and transformed into) life." Believers shrink from, not the consequences, but the mere act of dying; especially as believing in the possibility of their being found alive at the Lord's coming (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.15">1Th 4:15</reference>), and so of having their mortal body absorbed into the immortal without death. Faith does not divest us of all natural feeling, but subordinates it to higher feeling. Scripture gives no sanction to the contempt for the body expressed by philosophers. <div eID="gen34294" type="x-p"/>
entries.15faa95edd6abcf53173cc5c9ec05274869f5951: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17249"/><div sID="gen34295" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17249"/><hi type="bold">5. wrought us--</hi>framed us by redemption, justification, and sanctification.<div eID="gen34295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34296" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the selfsame thing--</hi>"unto" it; namely, unto what is mortal of us being swallowed up in life (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.4">2Co 5:4</reference>).<div eID="gen34296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34297" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who also--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "also."<div eID="gen34297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earnest of the Spirit--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.22">2Co 1:22</reference>). It is the Spirit (as "the first-fruits") who creates in us the groaning desire for our coming deliverance and glory (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.23">Ro 8:23</reference>). <div eID="gen34298" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e1433fb773f7cbbc7e7624aca99e921b1d340c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17250"/><div sID="gen34299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17250"/>6. Translate as Greek, "Being therefore always confident and knowing," &c. He had intended to have made the verb to this nominative, "we are willing" (rather, "well content"), but digressing on the word "confident" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.6">2Co 5:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.7">7</reference>), he resumes the word in a different form, namely, as an assertion: "We are confident and well content." "Being confident ... we are confident" may be the Hebraic idiom of emphasis; as <reference osisRef="Acts.7.34">Ac 7:34</reference>, Greek, "Having seen, I have seen," that is, I have surely seen.<div eID="gen34299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">always--</hi>under all trials. Bengel makes the contrast between "always confident" and "confident" especially at the prospect of being "absent from the body." We are confident as well at all times, as also most of all in the hope of a blessed departure.<div eID="gen34300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34301" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whilst ... at home ... absent--</hi>Translate as Greek, "While we sojourn in our home in the body, we are away from our home in the Lord." The image from a "house" is retained (compare <reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>; He 11:13-16; 13:14). <div eID="gen34301" type="x-p"/>
entries.03fb7105c4034d1deab3bdb187ece4a261d5f8b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17251"/><div sID="gen34302" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17251"/><hi type="bold">7. we walk--</hi>in our Christian course here on earth.<div eID="gen34302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34303" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not by sight--</hi>Greek, "not by appearance." Our life is governed by faith in our immortal hope; not by the outward specious appearance of present things [Tittmann, Greek Synonyms of the New Testament]. Compare "apparently," the Septuagint, "by appearance," <reference osisRef="Num.12.8">Nu 12:8</reference>. Wahl supports English Version. <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.18">2Co 4:18</reference> also confirms it (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.24">Ro 8:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">1Co 13:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.13">13</reference>). God has appointed in this life faith for our great duty, and in the next, vision for our reward [South] (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.8">1Pe 1:8</reference>). <div eID="gen34303" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c30dc8da5fc900195edb6bc38d877116f97d461: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17252"/><div sID="gen34304" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17252"/><hi type="bold">8. willing--</hi>literally, "well content." Translate also, "To go (literally, migrate) from our home in the body, and to come to our home with the Lord." We should prefer to be found alive at the Lord's coming, and to be clothed upon with our heavenly body (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.2-2Cor.5.4">2Co 5:2-4</reference>). But feeling, as we do, the sojourn in the body to be a separation from our true home "with the Lord," we prefer even dissolution by death, so that in the intermediate disembodied state we may go to be "with the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.23">Php 1:23</reference>). "To be with Christ" (the disembodied state) is distinguished from Christ's coming to take us to be with Him in soul and body (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.14-1Thess.4.17">1Th 4:14-17</reference>, "with the Lord"). Perhaps the disembodied spirits of believers have fulness of communion with Christ unseen; but not the mutual recognition of one another, until clothed with their visible bodies at the resurrection (compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13-1Thess.4.17">1Th 4:13-17</reference>), when they shall with joy recognize Christ's image in each other perfect. <div eID="gen34304" type="x-p"/>
entries.be4109b6d38ac2cf5389683626d9e1a1f2d63884: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17253"/><div sID="gen34305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17253"/><hi type="bold">9. Wherefore--</hi>with such a sure "confidence" of being blessed, whether we die before, or be found alive at Christ's coming.<div eID="gen34305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we labour--</hi>literally, "make it our ambition"; the only lawful ambition.<div eID="gen34306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34307" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whether present or absent--</hi>whether we be found at His coming present in the body, or absent from it.<div eID="gen34307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">accepted--</hi>Greek, "well-pleasing." <div eID="gen34308" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e58ce4361e2b11cc53d209b7c2e23eeee8a466c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17254"/><div sID="gen34309" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17254"/><hi type="bold">10. appear--</hi>rather, "be made manifest," namely, in our true character. So "appear," Greek, "be manifested" (<reference osisRef="Col.3.4">Col 3:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">1Co 4:5</reference>). We are at all times, even now, manifest to God; then we shall be so to the assembled intelligent universe and to ourselves: for the judgment shall be not only in order to assign the everlasting portion to each, but to vindicate God's righteousness, so that it shall be manifest to all His creatures, and even to the conscience of the sinner himself.<div eID="gen34309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receive--</hi>His reward of grace proportioned to "the things done," &c. (<reference osisRef="2Cor.9.6-2Cor.9.9">2Co 9:6-9</reference>; 2Jo 8). Though salvation be of grace purely, independent of works, the saved may have a greater or less reward, according as he lives to, and labors for, Christ more or less. Hence there is scope for the holy "ambition" (see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.9">2Co 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">He 6:10</reference>). This verse guards against the Corinthians supposing that all share in the house "from heaven" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2Co 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.2">2</reference>). There shall be a searching judgment which shall sever the bad from the good, according to their respective, deeds, the motive of the deeds being taken into account, not the mere external act; faith and love to God are the sole motives recognized by God as sound and good (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.36">Mt 12:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.37">37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.35-Matt.25.45">25:35-45</reference>),<div eID="gen34310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34311" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">done in his body--</hi>The Greek may be, "by the instrumentality of the body"; but English Version is legitimate (compare Greek, <reference osisRef="Rom.2.27">Ro 2:27</reference>). Justice requires that substantially the same body which has been the instrument of the unbelievers' sin, should be the object of punishment. A proof of the essential identity of the natural and the resurrection body. <div eID="gen34311" type="x-p"/>
entries.2323905bdd634eba3e0817fd12ec193c9445905b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17255"/><div sID="gen34312" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17255"/><hi type="bold">11. terror of the Lord--</hi>the coming judgment, so full of terrors to unbelievers [Estius]. Ellicott and Alford, after Grotius and Bengel, translate, "The fear of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.1">2Co 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.13">Ec 12:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.9.31">Ac 9:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.18">Ro 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.21">Ep 5:21</reference>).<div eID="gen34312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">persuade--</hi>Ministers should use the terrors of the Lord to persuade men, not to rouse their enmity (Jude 23). Bengel, Estius, and Alford explain: "Persuade men" (by our whole lives, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.13">2Co 5:13</reference>), namely, of our integrity as ministers. But this would have been expressed after "persuade," had it been the sense. The connection seems as follows: He had been accused of seeking to please and win men, he therefore says (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">Ga 1:10</reference>), "It is as knowing the terror (or fear) of the Lord that we persuade men; but (whether men who hear our preaching recognize our sincerity or not) we are made manifest unto God as acting on such motives (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2Co 4:2</reference>); and I trust also in your consciences." Those so "manifested" need have no "terror" as to their being "manifested (English Version, 'appear') before the judgment-seat" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10">2Co 5:10</reference>). <div eID="gen34313" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e57b9979333b81bde816efa3f122c79798d595e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17256"/><div sID="gen34314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17256"/><hi type="bold">12. For--</hi>the reason why he leaves the manifestation of his sincerity in preaching to their consciences (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">2Co 3:1</reference>), namely, his not wishing to "commend" himself again.<div eID="gen34314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">occasion to glory--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.14">2Co 1:14</reference>), namely, as to our sincerity.<div eID="gen34315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in appearance--</hi>Greek, "face" (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.7">1Sa 16:7</reference>). The false teachers gloried in their outward appearance, and in external recommendations (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.18">2Co 11:18</reference>) their learning, eloquence, wisdom, riches, not in vital religion in their heart. Their conscience does not attest their inward sincerity, as mine does (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2Co 1:12</reference>). <div eID="gen34316" type="x-p"/>
entries.0fe7357d82328f8720aaeebddb6005d76bc2b1ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17257"/><div sID="gen34317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17257"/><hi type="bold">13. be--</hi>rather as Greek, "have been." The contrast is between the single act implied by the past tense, "If we have ever been beside ourselves," and the habitual state implied by the present, "Or whether we be sober," that is, of sound mind. beside ourselves--The accusation brought by Festus against him (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.24">Ac 26:24</reference>). The holy enthusiasm with which he spake of what God effected by His apostolic ministry, seemed to many to be boasting madness.<div eID="gen34317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sober--</hi>humbling myself before you, and not using my apostolic power and privileges.<div eID="gen34318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to God ... for your cause--</hi>The glorifying of his office was not for his own, but for God's glory. The abasing of himself was in adaptation to their infirmity, to gain them to Christ (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.22">1Co 9:22</reference>). <div eID="gen34319" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b2746560d0a61252f7e7de28cd03f31c7499cc9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17258"/><div sID="gen34320" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17258"/><hi type="bold">14. For--</hi>Accounting for his being "beside himself" with enthusiasm: the love of Christ towards us (in His death for us, the highest proof of it, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.6-Rom.5.8">Ro 5:6-8</reference>), producing in turn love in us to Him, and not mere "terror" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.11">2Co 5:11</reference>).<div eID="gen34320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">constraineth us--</hi>with irresistible power limits us to the one great object to the exclusion of other considerations. The Greek implies to compress forcibly the energies into one channel. Love is jealous of any rival object engrossing the soul (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1-2Cor.11.3">2Co 11:1-3</reference>).<div eID="gen34321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34322" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because we thus judge--</hi>literally, "(as) having judged thus"; implying a judgment formed at conversion, and ever since regarded as a settled truth.<div eID="gen34322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that if--</hi>that is, that since. But the oldest manuscripts omit "if." "That one died for all (Greek, 'in behalf of all')." Thus the following clause will be, "Therefore all (literally, 'the all,' namely, for whom He 'died') died." His dying is just the same as if they all died; and in their so dying, they died to sin and self, that they might live to God their Redeemer, whose henceforth they are (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.2-Rom.6.11">Ro 6:2-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.3">Col 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.1-1Pet.4.3">1Pe 4:1-3</reference>). <div eID="gen34323" type="x-p"/>
entries.55c3e0c41ba6470e24bdb0cc226bcdb73a013eb4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17259"/><div sID="gen34324" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17259"/><hi type="bold">15. they which live--</hi>in the present life (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">2Co 4:11</reference>, "we which live") [Alford]; or, they who are thus indebted to Him for life of soul as well as body [Menochius].<div eID="gen34324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34325" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">died for them--</hi>He does not add, "rose again for them," a phrase not found in Paul's language [Bengel]. He died in their stead, He arose again for their good, "for (the effecting of) their justification" (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">Ro 4:25</reference>), and that He might be their Lord (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.7-Rom.14.9">Ro 14:7-9</reference>). Ellicott and Alford join "for them" with both "died" and "rose again"; as Christ's death is our death, so His resurrection is our resurrection; Greek, "Who for them died and rose again."<div eID="gen34325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not henceforth--</hi>Greek, "no longer"; namely, now that His death for them has taken place, and that they know that His death saves them from death eternal, and His resurrection life brings spiritual and everlasting life to them. <div eID="gen34326" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee7365bf715449ed2d14b236876214639dab863f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17260"/><div sID="gen34327" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17260"/><hi type="bold">16. Wherefore--</hi>because of our settled judgment (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.14">2Co 5:14</reference>),<div eID="gen34327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">henceforth--</hi>since our knowing Christ's constraining love in His death for us.<div eID="gen34328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34329" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know we no man after the flesh--</hi>that is, according to his mere worldly and external relations (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.18">2Co 11:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.15">Joh 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.4">Php 3:4</reference>), as distinguished from what he is according to the Spirit, as a "new creature" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.17">2Co 5:17</reference>). For instance, the outward distinctions of Jew or Gentile, rich or poor, slave or free, learned or unlearned, are lost sight of in the higher life of those who are dead in Christ's death, and alive with Him in the new life of His resurrection (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.6">Ga 2:6</reference>; 3:28).<div eID="gen34329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yea, though--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "if even."<div eID="gen34330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34331" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">known Christ after the flesh--</hi>Paul when a Jew had looked for a temporal reigning, not a spiritual, Messiah. (He says "Christ," not Jesus: for he had not known personally Jesus in the days of His flesh, but he had looked for Christ or the Messiah). When once he was converted he no longer "conferred with flesh and blood" (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.16">Ga 1:16</reference>). He had this advantage over the Twelve, that as one born out of due time he had never known Christ save in His heavenly life. To the Twelve it was "expedient that Christ should go away" that the Comforter should come, and so they might know Christ in the higher spiritual aspect and in His new life-giving power, and not merely "after the flesh," in the carnal aspect of Him (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.9-Rom.6.11">Ro 6:9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.45">1Co 15:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1Pe 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.1">4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2</reference>). Doubtless Judaizing Christians at Corinth prided themselves on the mere fleshly (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.18">2Co 11:18</reference>) advantage of their belonging to Israel, the nation of Christ, or on their having seen Him in the flesh, and thence claimed superiority over others as having a nearer connection with Him (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.12">2Co 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.7">2Co 10:7</reference>). Paul here shows the true aim should be to know Him spiritually as new creatures (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.15">2Co 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.17">17</reference>), and that outward relations towards Him profit nothing (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.19-Luke.18.21">Lu 18:19-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.7">Joh 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.16.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.3-Phil.3.10">Php 3:3-10</reference>). This is at variance with both Romish Mariolatry and transubstantiation. Two distinct Greek verbs are used here for "know"; the first ("know we no man") means "to be personally acquainted with"; the latter ("known Christ ... know ... more") is to recognize, or estimate. Paul's estimate of Christ, or the expected Messiah, was carnal, but is so now no more. <div eID="gen34331" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2ae442d3740dc2c7846d475a677d604dc0e5a44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17261"/><div sID="gen34332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17261"/><hi type="bold">17. Therefore--</hi>connected with the words in <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.16">2Co 5:16</reference>, "We know Christ no more after the flesh." As Christ has entered on His new heavenly life by His resurrection and ascension, so all who are "in Christ" (that is, united to Him by faith as the branch is In the vine) are new creatures (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.9-Rom.6.11">Ro 6:9-11</reference>). "New" in the Greek implies a new nature quite different from anything previously existing, not merely recent, which is expressed by a different Greek word (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.15">Ga 6:15</reference>).<div eID="gen34332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">creature--</hi>literally, "creation," and so the creature resulting from the creation (compare <reference osisRef="John.3.3">Joh 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.3.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Ep 2:10</reference>; 4:23; <reference osisRef="Col.3.10">Col 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">11</reference>). As we are "in Christ," so "God was in Christ" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Co 5:19</reference>): hence He is Mediator between God and us.<div eID="gen34333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">old things--</hi>selfish, carnal views (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.16">2Co 5:16</reference>) of ourselves, of other men, and of Christ.<div eID="gen34334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34335" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passed away--</hi>spontaneously, like the snow of early spring [Bengel] before the advancing sun.<div eID="gen34335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behold--</hi>implying an allusion to <reference osisRef="Isa.43.19">Is 43:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">65:17</reference>. <div eID="gen34336" type="x-p"/>
entries.52ef78b8a6dbbf195a8527aee0f8ad5c11efc9be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17262"/><div sID="gen34337" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17262"/><hi type="bold">18. all--</hi>Greek, "THE."<div eID="gen34337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things--</hi>all our privileges in this new creation (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.14">2Co 5:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen34338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reconciled us--</hi>that is, restored us ("the world," <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Co 5:19</reference>) to His favor by satisfying the claims of justice against us. Our position judicially considered in the eye of the law is altered, not as though the mediation of Christ had made a change in God's character, nor as if the love of God was produced by the mediation of Christ; nay, the mediation and sacrifice of Christ was the provision of God's love, not its moving cause (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.32">Ro 8:32</reference>). Christ's blood was the price paid at the expense of God Himself, and was required to reconcile the exercise of mercy with justice, not as separate, but as the eternally harmonious attributes in the one and the same God (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.25">Ro 3:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.26">26</reference>). The Greek "reconcile" is reciprocally used as in the Hebrew Hithpahel conjugation, appease, obtain the favor of. <reference osisRef="Matt.5.24">Mt 5:24</reference>, "Be reconciled to thy brother"; that is, take measures that he be reconciled to thee, as well as thou to him, as the context proves. Diallagethi, however (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.24">Mt 5:24</reference>), implying mutual reconciliation, is distinct from Katallagethi here, the latter referring to the change of status wrought in one of the two parties. The manner of God reconciling the world to Himself is implied (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Co 5:19</reference>), namely, by His "not imputing their trespasses to them." God not merely, as subsequently, reconciles the world by inducing them to lay aside their enmity, but in the first instance, does so by satisfying His own justice and righteous enmity against sin (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.11">Psa 7:11</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.4">1Sa 29:4</reference>, "Reconcile himself unto his master"; not remove his own anger against his master, but his master's against him [Archbishop Magee, Atonement]. The reconciling of men to God by their laying aside their enmity is the consequence of God laying aside His just enmity against their sin, and follows at <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.20">2Co 5:20</reference>.<div eID="gen34339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34340" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to us--</hi>ministers (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Co 5:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.20">20</reference>). <div eID="gen34340" type="x-p"/>
entries.16b03f1f24469a626cbfb854c78494a9b5e7a8d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17263"/><div sID="gen34341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17263"/><hi type="bold">19. God was in Christ, reconciling--</hi>that is, God was BY Christ (in virtue of Christ's intervention) reconciling," &c. Was reconciling" implies the time when the act of reconciliation was being carried into effect (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>), namely, when "God made Jesus, who knew no sin, to be sin for us." The compound of "was" and the participle "reconciling," instead of the imperfect (Greek), may also imply the continuous purpose of God, from before the foundation of the world, to reconcile man to Himself, whose fall was foreseen. The expression " IN Christ" for "by Christ" may be used to imply additionally that God was IN Christ (<reference osisRef="John.10.38">Joh 10:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.10">14:10</reference>), and so by Christ (the God-man) was reconciling ... The Greek for "by" or "through" Christ (the best manuscripts omit "Jesus"), <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18">2Co 5:18</reference>, is different. "In" must mean here in the person of Christ. The Greek Katallasson implies "changing" or altering the judicial status from one of condemnation to one of justification. The atonement (at-one-ment), or reconciliation, is the removal of the bar to peace and acceptance with a holy God, which His righteousness interposed against our sin. The first step towards restoring peace between us and God was on God's side (<reference osisRef="John.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference>). The change therefore now to be effected must be on the part of offending man, God the offended One being already reconciled. It is man, not God, who now needs to be reconciled, and to lay aside his enmity against God (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.10">Ro 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.11">11</reference>). ("We have received the atonement" [Greek, reconciliation], cannot mean "We have received the laying aside of our own enmity"). Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">Ro 3:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.25">25</reference>.<div eID="gen34341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the world--</hi>all men (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.2">1Jo 2:2</reference>). The manner of the reconciling is by His "not imputing to men their trespasses," but imputing them to Christ the Sin-bearer. There is no incongruity that a father should be offended with that son whom he loveth, and at that time offended with him when he loveth him. So, though God loved men whom He created, yet He was offended with them when they sinned, and gave His Son to suffer for them, that through that Son's obedience He might be reconciled to them (reconcile them to Himself, that is, restore them WITH JUSTICE to His favor) [Bishop Pearson, Exposition of the Creed].<div eID="gen34342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath committed unto us--</hi>Greek, "hath put into our hands." "Us," that is, ministers. <div eID="gen34343" type="x-p"/>
entries.c82602138ac57a0ccb48f1f419c9424b3034de96: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17264"/><div sID="gen34344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17264"/><hi type="bold">20. for Christ ... in Christ's stead--</hi>The Greek of both is the same: translate in both cases "on Christ's behalf."<div eID="gen34344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34345" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beseech ... pray--</hi>rather, "entreat [plead with you] ... beseech." Such "beseeching" is uncommon in the case of "ambassadors," who generally stand on their dignity (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.2">2Co 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.6">1Th 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen34345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be ye reconciled to God--</hi>English Version here inserts "ye," which is not in the original, and which gives the wrong impression, as if it were emphatic thus: God is reconciled to you, be ye reconciled to God. The Greek expresses rather, God was the RECONCILER in Christ ... let this reconciliation then have its designed effect. Be reconciled to God, that is, let God reconcile you to Himself (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18">2Co 5:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">19</reference>). <div eID="gen34346" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f1ee5c3055d0e4b193471032bca07536b147ecc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17265"/><div sID="gen34347" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17265"/><hi type="bold">21. For--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts. The grand reason why they should be reconciled to God, namely, the great atonement in Christ provided by God, is stated without the "for" as being part of the message of reconciliation (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Co 5:19</reference>).<div eID="gen34347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>God.<div eID="gen34348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin--</hi>not a sin offering, which would destroy the antithesis to "righteousness," and would make "sin" be used in different senses in the same sentence: not a sinful person, which would be untrue, and would require in the antithesis "righteous men," not "righteousness"; but "sin," that is, the representative Sin-bearer (vicariously) of the aggregate sin of all men past, present, and future. The sin of the world is one, therefore the singular, not the plural, is used; though its manifestations are manifold (<reference osisRef="John.1.29">Joh 1:29</reference>). "Behold the Lamb of God, that taketh away the SIN of the world." Compare "made a curse for us," <reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">Ga 3:13</reference>.<div eID="gen34349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for us--</hi>Greek, "in our behalf." Compare <reference osisRef="John.3.14">Joh 3:14</reference>, Christ being represented by the brazen serpent, the form, but not the substance, of the old serpent. At His death on the cross the sin-bearing for us was consummated.<div eID="gen34350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34351" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knew no sin--</hi>by personal experience (<reference osisRef="John.8.46">Joh 8:46</reference>) [Alford]. <reference osisRef="Heb.7.26">He 7:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.22">1Pe 2:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.5">1Jo 3:5</reference>.<div eID="gen34351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">might be made--</hi>not the same Greek as the previous "made." Rather, "might become."<div eID="gen34352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the righteousness of God--</hi>Not merely righteous, but righteousness itself; not merely righteousness, but the righteousness of God, because Christ is God, and what He is we are (<reference osisRef="1John.4.17">1Jo 4:17</reference>), and He is "made of God unto us righteousness." As our sin is made over to Him, so His righteousness to us (in His having fulfilled all the righteousness of the law for us all, as our representative, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jr 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>). The innocent was punished voluntarily as if guilty, that the guilty might be gratuitously rewarded as if innocent (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.24">1Pe 2:24</reference>). "Such are we in the sight of God the Father, as is the very Son of God himself" [Hooker].<div eID="gen34353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in him--</hi>by virtue of our standing in Him, and in union with Him [Alford]. <chapter eID="2Cor.5"/>

entries.bf5639eaeb03707128021027a89eb583be59ad3f: <div eID="gen48942" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen48943" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen48944" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen48944" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen48943" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen48945" type="x-p"/> The apostle's strong hope of eternal glory, and earnest longings after that state of blessedness, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1-2Cor.5.4">2Cor 5:1-4</reference>. The assurance that he had of it from the Holy Spirit, and his carefulness to be always found pleasing to the Lord, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.5-2Cor.5.9">2Cor 5:5-9</reference>. All must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10">2Cor 5:10</reference>. Knowing that this awful event must take place, he labored to convince men of the necessity of being prepared to meet the Lord, being influenced to this work by his love of Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.11-2Cor.5.13">2Cor 5:11-13</reference>. Jesus Christ having died for all, is a proof that all were dead, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.14">2Cor 5:14</reference>. Those for whom he died should live to him, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.15">2Cor 5:15</reference>. We should know no man after the flesh, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.16">2Cor 5:16</reference>. They who are in Christ are new creatures, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.17">2Cor 5:17</reference>. The glorious ministry of reconciliation, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18-2Cor.5.21">2Cor 5:18-21</reference>. <div eID="gen48945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48946" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen48946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48947" type="x-p"/> If our earthly house of this tabernacle - By earthly house, the apostle most evidently means the body in which the soul is represented as dwelling or sojourning for a time, and from which it is to be liberated at death; for as death dissolves the tabernacle, it can then be no habitation for the soul. The apostle also alludes here to the ancient Jewish tabernacle, which, on all removals of the congregation, was dissolved and taken in pieces; and the ark of the covenant, covered with its own curtains, was carried by itself; and when they came to the place of rest, then the dissolved parts of the tabernacle were put together as before. When we consider this simile in connection with the doctrine of the resurrection, which the apostle has treated so much at large in these epistles, and which he keeps constantly in view, then we shall see that he intends to convey the following meaning: that as the tabernacle was taken down in order to be again put together, so the body is to be dissolved, in order to be re-edified; that as the ark of the covenant subsisted by itself, while the tabernacle was down, so can the soul when separated from the body; that as the ark had then its own veil for its covering, <reference osisRef="Exo.40.21">Exo 40:21</reference>, so the soul is to have some vehicle in which it shall subsist till it receives its body at the resurrection. <div eID="gen48947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48948" type="x-p"/> A building of God - Some think this refers to a certain celestial vehicle with which God invests holy souls on their dismissal from the body; others suppose it relates to the resurrection body; and some imagine that it relates merely to the state of blessedness which the saints shall possess in the kingdom of glory. See the following note.
entries.cdce8ed1f8aa883b1395c2ec2247c1747b5c9941: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen48948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48949" type="x-p"/> For in this we groan - While in this state, and in this body, we are encompassed with many infirmities, and exposed to many trials, so that life is a state of discipline and affliction, and every thing within and around us says, "Arise and depart, for this is not your rest!" Those who apply these words to what they call the apostle's sense of indwelling sin, abuse the passage. There is nothing of the kind either mentioned or intended. <div eID="gen48949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48950" type="x-p"/> Desiring to be clothed upon with our house - This and the following verses are, in themselves, exceedingly obscure, and can be only interpreted by considering that the expressions used by the apostle are all Jewish, and should be interpreted according to their use of them. Schoettgen has entered largely into the argument here employed by the apostle, and brought forth much useful information. <div eID="gen48950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48951" type="x-p"/> He observes, <div eID="gen48951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48952" type="x-p"/> 1. That the Hebrew word לבש labash, which answers to the apostle's ενδυσασθαι, to be clothed, signifies to be surrounded, covered, or invested with any thing. So, to be clothed with the uncircumcision, signifies to be uncircumcised. Yalcut Rubeni, fol. 163. <div eID="gen48952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48953" type="x-p"/> On the words, <reference osisRef="Exo.24.18">Exo 24:18</reference>, Moses went into the midst of the cloud, and gat him up into the mount, Sohar Exod., fol. 77, has these words, He went into the midst of the cloud, as if one put on a garment; so he was Clothed with the Cloud. Sohar Levit., fol. 29: "The righteous are in the terrestrial paradise, where their souls are clothed with the lucid crown;" i.e. they are surrounded, encompassed with light, etc. <div eID="gen48953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48954" type="x-p"/> 2. The word בית beith, House, in Hebrew often denotes a cover, case, or clothing. So, in the Targum of Onkelos, בית אפי beith appei, the House or the Face, is a veil; and so בית אצבעים beith etsbaim, the House of the Fingers, and בית יד beith yad, the House of the Hand, signify gloves; בית רגלים beith regalim, the House of the Feet, shoes. Therefore, οικητηριον - επενδυσασθαι, to be clothed on with a house, may signify any particular qualities of the soul; what we, following the very same form of speech, call a habit, i.e. a coat or vestment. So we say the man has got a habit of vice, a habit of virtue, a habit of swearing, of humility, etc., etc. <div eID="gen48954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48955" type="x-p"/> 3. The Jews attribute garments to the soul, both in this and the other world; and as they hold that all human souls pre-exist, they say that, previously to their being appointed to bodies, they have a covering which answers the same end to them before they come into life as their bodies do afterwards. And they state that the design of God in sending souls into the world is, that they may get themselves a garment by the study of the law and good works. See several proofs in Schoettgen. <div eID="gen48955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48956" type="x-p"/> 4. It is plain, also, that by this garment or covering of the soul they mean simply what we understand by acquiring the image of God - being made holy. This image they assert "Adam lost by his fall, and they represent man in a sinful state as being naked." So they represent the Israelites before their making the molten calf, as having received holy garments from Mount Sinai; but afterwards, having worshipped the calf, they were stripped of these, and left naked. <div eID="gen48956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48957" type="x-p"/> 5. But notwithstanding they speak of this clothing as implying righteous and holy dispositions, and heavenly qualities, yet they all agree in assigning certain vehicles to separate spirits, in which they act; but of these vehicles they have strange notions; yet they acknowledge that without them, whether they be of light, fire, etc., or whatever else, they cannot see and contemplate the Supreme Wisdom. In Synopsis Sohar, page 137, we have these words: "When the time draws near in which a man is to depart from this world, the angel of death takes off his mortal garment and clothes him with one from paradise, in which he may see and contemplate the Supreme Wisdom; and therefore the angel of death is said to be very kind to man, because he takes off from him the garment of this world, and clothes him with a much more precious one prepared in paradise." <div eID="gen48957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48958" type="x-p"/> When the apostle says that they earnestly desired to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven, he certainly means that the great concern of all the genuine followers of God was to be fully prepared to enjoy the beatific vision of their Maker and Redeemer.
entries.cecc4a412d28451b889a241d7b33c0de23681005: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen48958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48959" type="x-p"/> If so be that being clothed - That is, fully prepared in this life for the glory of God; <div eID="gen48959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48960" type="x-p"/> We shall not be found naked - Destitute in that future state of that Divine image which shall render us capable of enjoying an endless glory.
entries.4a67f8e186dd034cbe09f6d54ea0c0c013191cca: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen48960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48961" type="x-p"/> For we that are in this tabernacle - We who are in this state of trial and difficulty do groan, being burdened; as if he had said: The whole of human life is a state of suffering, and especially our lot; who are troubled on every side, perplexed, persecuted, cast down, bearing about in the body the dying of our Lord Jesus, and being always delivered unto death on the account of Jesus, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8-2Cor.4.11">2Cor 4:8-11</reference>. These were sufficient burdens, and sufficient causes of groaning. <div eID="gen48961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48962" type="x-p"/> Not for that we would be unclothed - We do not desire death, nor to die, even with the full prospect of eternal glory before our eyes, an hour before that time which God in his wisdom has assigned. <div eID="gen48962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48963" type="x-p"/> But clothed upon - To have the fullest preparation for eternal glory. We wish not to die, whatever tribulation we may be called to pass through, till the whole will of God is accomplished in us and by us. <div eID="gen48963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48964" type="x-p"/> That mortality might be swallowed up of life - Being fully prepared for the eternal state we shall scarcely be said to die, all that is mortal being absorbed and annihilated by immortality and glory. See the notes on <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51-1Cor.15.56">1Cor 15:51-56</reference> (note). From the use of these expressions among the Jews, this seems to be the general meaning of the apostle.
entries.6adfd65c1903614e18f0320cd3067cfed85353a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen48964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48965" type="x-p"/> Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing - God has given us our being and our body for this very purpose, that both might be made immortal, and both be glorified together. Or, God himself has given us this insatiable hungering and thirsting after righteousness and immortality.
