19. God was in Christ. Some take this as meaning simply — God reconciled the world to himself in Christ; but the meaning is fuller and more comprehensive — first, that God was in Christ; and, secondly, that he reconciled the world to himself by his intercession. It is also of the Father that this is affirmed; for it were an improper expression, were you to understand it as meaning, that the divine nature of Christ was in him.
“Car ce seroit improprement, de dire que la nature Diuine de Christ estoit en Christ;” — “For it were to speak improperly, to say that the Divine nature of Christ was in Christ.”
The Father, therefore, was in the Son, in accordance with that statement —
I am in the Father, and the Father in me. (John 10:38.)
Therefore he that hath the Son, hath the Father also. For Paul has made use of this expression with this view — that we may learn to be satisfied with Christ alone, because in him we find also God the Father, as he truly communicates himself to us by him. Hence the expression is equivalent to this — “Whereas God had withdrawn to a distance from us, he has drawn near to us in Christ, and thus Christ has become to us the true Emmanuel, and his coming is God’s drawing near to men.”
The second part of the statement points out the office of Christ — his being our propitiation, (1 John 2:2,) because out of Him, God is displeased with us all, inasmuch as we have revolted from righteousness.
“De iustice et obeissance;” — “From righteousness and obedience.”
For what purpose, then, has God appeared to men in Christ? For the purpose of reconciliation — that, hostilities being removed, those who were aliens, might be adopted as sons. Now, although Christ’s coming as our Redeemer originated in the fountain of Divine love towards us, yet until men perceive that God has been propitiated by the Mediator, there must of necessity be a variance remaining, with respect to them, which shuts them out from access to God. On this point we shall speak more fully ere long.
Not imputing to them. Mark, in what way men return into favor with God — when they are regarded as righteous, by obtaining the remission of their sins. For so long as God imputes to us our sins, He must of necessity regard us with abhorrence; for he cannot be friendly or propitious to sinners. But this statement may seem to be at variance with what is said elsewhere — that, we were loved by Him before the creation of the world, (Ephesians 1:4,) and still more with what he says, (John 3:16,) that the love, which he exercised towards us was the reason, why He expiated our sins by Christ, for the cause always goes before its effect. I answer, that we were loved before the creation of the world, but it was only in Christ In the mean time, however, I confess, that the love of God was first in point of time, and of order, too, as to God, but with respect to us, the commencement of his love has its foundation in the sacrifice of Christ. For when we contemplate God without a Mediator, we cannot conceive of Him otherwise than as angry with us: a Mediator interposed between us, makes us feel, that He is pacified towards us. As, however, this also is necessary to be known by us — that Christ came forth to us from the fountain of God’s free mercy, the Scripture explicitly teaches both — that the anger of the Father has been appeased by the sacrifice of the Son, and that the Son has been offered up for the expiation of the sins of men on this ground — because God, exercising compassion towards them, receives them, on the ground of such a pledge, into favor.
“C’est d’ autant que Dieu ayant compassion d’eux, a voulu que ceste mort fust le gage et le moyen par lequel il les receuroit en grace;” — “It is, because God, having compassion upon them, determined that this death should be the pledge and means, by which he would receive them into favor.”
The whole may be summed up thus: “Where sin is, there the anger of God is, and therefore God is not propitious to us without, or before, his blotting out our sins, by not imputing them. As our consciences cannot apprehend this benefit,
“Et en estre participantes;” — “And be partakers of it.”
otherwise than through the intervention of Christ’s sacrifice, it is not without good reason, that Paul makes that the commencement and cause of reconciliation, with regard to us.
And hath committed to us. Again he repeats, that a commission has been given to the ministers of the gospel to communicate to us this grace. For it might be objected, “Where is Christ now, the peacemaker between God and us? At what a distance he resides from us!” He says, therefore, that as he has once suffered,
“Comme il a souffert la mort vne fois;” — “As he has suffered death once.”
(1 Peter 3:18,) so he daily presents to us the fruit of his suffering through means of the Gospel, which he designed, should be in the world,
“Lequel il a voulu estre gardé et publié au monde;” — “Which he designed, should be maintained and published in the world.”
as a sure and authentic register of the reconciliation, that has once been effected. It is the part of ministers, therefore, to apply to us, so to speak, the fruit of Christ’s death.
Lest, however, any one should dream of a magical application, such as Papists contrive,
See Calvin on John, vol. 2, p. 272. — Ed
we must carefully observe what he immediately subjoins — that it consists wholly in the preaching of the Gospel. For the Pope, along with his priests, makes use of this pretext for giving a color of warrant for the whole of that wicked and execrable system of merchandise, which they carry on, in connection with the salvation of souls. “The Lord,” say they, “has furnished us with a commission and authority to forgive sins.” This I acknowledge, provided they discharge that embassy, of which Paul here makes mention. The absolution, however, which they make use of in the Papacy, is entirely magical; and besides, they inclose pardon of sins in lead and parchment, or they connect it with fictitious and frivolous superstitions. What resemblance do all these things bear to the appointment of Christ? Hence the ministers of the Gospel restore us to the favor of God in a right and orderly manner, when they bear testimony to us by means of the Gospel as to the favor of God having been procured for us. Let this testimony be removed, and nothing remains but mere imposture. Beware, then, of placing even the smallest drop of your confidence on any thing apart from the Gospel.
I do not, indeed, deny, that the grace of Christ is applied to us in the sacraments, and that our reconciliation with God is then confirmed in our consciences; but, as the testimony of the Gospel is engraven upon the sacraments, they are not to be judged of separately by themselves, but must be taken in connection with the Gospel, of which they are appendages. In fine, the ministers of the Church are ambassadors, for testifying and proclaiming the benefit of reconciliation, only on this condition — that they speak from the Gospel, as from an authentic register.
entries.06352935b111e7374e13d2b75b62bdd22cac9ec0: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.5.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.5.20" sID="gen121720" type="section"/> <div sID="gen121721" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20. </hi><hi type="italic">As if God did beseech you</hi> This is of no small importance for giving authority to the embassy: nay more, it is absolutely necessary, for who would rest upon the testimony of men, in reference to his eternal salvation? It is a matter of too much importance, to allow of our resting contented with the promise of men, without feeling assured that they are ordained by God, and that God speaks to us by them. This is the design of those commendations, with which Christ himself signalizes his Apostles:<div eID="gen121721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen121722" type="x-p"/>He that heareth you, heareth me, etc. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.10.16">Luke 10:16</reference>.)<div eID="gen121722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen121723" type="x-p"/>Whatsoever you shall loose on earth, shall be loosed in heaven, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.18.18">Matthew 18:18</reference>,)<div eID="gen121723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen121724" type="x-p"/>and the like.<div eID="gen121724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen121725" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">We entreat you, in Christ’s stead.</hi> Hence we infer, with what propriety Isaiah exclaims,<div eID="gen121725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen121726" type="x-p"/>How blessed are the feet of them that preach the Gospel!<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.52.7">Isaiah 52:7</reference>.)<div eID="gen121726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen121727" type="x-p"/>For that one thing, that is of itself sufficient for completing our felicity, and without which we are most miserable, is conferred upon us, only through means of the Gospel. If, however, this duty is enjoined upon all the ministers of the Church, in such a way, that he who does not discharge this embassy is not to be regarded either as an Apostle, or as a Pastor, we may very readily judge from this, as to the nature of the Pope’s entire hierarchy. They are desirous, indeed, to be looked upon as Apostles and Pastors; but as they are dumb idols, how will their boasting <note n="561"> <div sID="gen121728" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Leur vanterie orgueilleuse</foreign>;” — “Their haughty boasting.”<div eID="gen121728" type="x-p"/> </note> correspond with this passage of Paul’s writings. The word <hi type="italic">entreat </hi>is expressive of an unparalleled <note n="562"> <div sID="gen121729" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vne singuliere et inestimable louange</foreign>;” — “A singular and inestimable commendation.”<div eID="gen121729" type="x-p"/> </note> commendation of the grace of Christ, inasmuch as He stoops so low, that he does not disdain to <hi type="italic">entreat </hi>us. So much the less excusable is our depravity, if we do not, on meeting with such kindness, show ourselves teachable and compliant.<div eID="gen121727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen121730" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Be reconciled.</hi> It is to be observed, that Paul is here addressing himself to believers. He declares, that he brings to them every day this embassy. Christ therefore, did not suffer, merely that he might once expiate our sins, nor was the gospel appointed merely with a view to the pardon of those sins which we committed previously to baptism, but that, as we daily sin, so we might, also, by a daily remission, be received by God into his favor. For this is a continued embassy, <note n="563"> <div sID="gen121731" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vne ambassade et commission perpetuelle</foreign>;” — “A perpetual embassy and commission.”<div eID="gen121731" type="x-p"/> </note> which must be assiduously sounded forth in the Church, till the end of the world; and the gospel cannot be preached, unless remission of sins is promised.<div eID="gen121730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen121732" type="x-p"/>We have here an express and suitable declaration for refuting the impious tenet of Papists, which calls upon us to seek the remission of sins after Baptism from some other source, than from the expiation that was effected through the death of Christ. Now this doctrine is commonly held in all the schools of Popery — that, after baptism, we merit the remission of sins by penitence, through means of the aid of the <hi type="italic">keys,</hi> <note n="564"> <div sID="gen121733" type="x-p"/> The reader will find this tenet of Popery adverted to by Calvin at considerable length in the <hi type="italic">Institutes</hi>, volume 3 — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen121733" type="x-p"/> </note> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.16.19">Matthew 16:19</reference>,) — as if baptism itself could confer this <note n="565"> <div sID="gen121734" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La remission de nos pechez</foreign>;” — “The remission of our sins.”<div eID="gen121734" type="x-p"/> </note> upon us without penitence. By the term <hi type="italic">penitence, </hi>however, they mean <hi type="italic">satisfactions. </hi>But what does Paul say here? He calls us to go, not less <hi type="italic">after </hi>baptism, than <hi type="italic">before </hi>it, to the one expiation made by Christ, that we may know that we always obtain it gratuitously. Farther, all their prating as to the administration of the <hi type="italic">keys </hi>is to no purpose, inasmuch as they conceive of <hi type="italic">keys </hi>apart from the Gospel, while they are nothing else than that testimony of a gratuitous reconciliation, which is made to us in the Gospel.<div eID="gen121732" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.5.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen121720" osisID="2Cor.5.20" type="section"/>

21. Him who knew no sin. Do you observe, that, according to Paul, there is no return to favor with God, except what is founded on the sacrifice of Christ alone? Let us learn, therefore, to turn our views in that direction, whenever we desire to be absolved from guilt. He now teaches more clearly, what we adverted to above — that God is propitious to us, when he acknowledges us as righteous. For these two things are equivalent — that we are acceptable to God, and that we are regarded by him as righteous.
To know no sin is to be free from sin. He says, then, that Christ, while he was entirely exempt from sin, was made sin for us. It is commonly remarked, that sin here denotes an expiatory sacrifice for sin, and in the same way the Latin’s term it, piaculum
The Latin term piaculum is sometimes employed to denote a crime requiring expiation, and at other times, an expiatory victim. — Ed
Paul, too, has in this, and other passages, borrowed this phrase from the Hebrews, among whom אשם (asham) denotes an expiatory sacrifice, as well as an offense or crime.
Thus in Leviticus 5:6, אשם, (asham,) denotes a trespass-offering; and in the verse immediately following, it means an offense or trespass. See Calvin’s Institutes, volume 2. — Ed.
But the signification of this word, as well as the entire statement, will be better understood from a comparison of both parts of the antithesis. Sin is here contrasted with righteousness, when Paul teaches us, that we were made the righteousness of God, on the ground of Christ’s having been made sin. Righteousness, here, is not taken to denote a quality or habit, but by way of imputation, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness being reckoned to have been received by us. What, on the other hand, is denoted by sin? It is the guilt, on account of which we are arraigned at the bar of God. As, however, the curse of the individual was of old cast upon the victim, so Christ’s condemnation was our absolution, and with his stripes we are healed. (Isaiah 53:5.)
The righteousness of God in him In the first place, the righteousness of God is taken here to denote — not that which is given us by God, but that which is approved of by him, as in John 12:43, the glory of God means — that which is in estimation with him — the glory of men denotes the vain applause of the world. Farther, in Romans 3:23, when he says, that we have come short of the glory of God, he means, that there is nothing that we can glory in before God, for it is no very difficult matter to appear righteous before men, but it is a mere delusive appearance of righteousness, which becomes at last the ground of perdition. Hence, that is the only true righteousness, which is acceptable to God.
Let us now return to the contrast between righteousness and sin How are we righteous in the sight of God? It is assuredly in the same respect in which Christ was a sinner. For he assumed in a manner our place, that he might be a criminal in our room, and might be dealt with as a sinner, not for his own offenses, but for those of others, inasmuch as he was pure and exempt from every fault, and might endure the punishment that was due to us — not to himself. It is in the same manner, assuredly, that we are now righteous in him — not in respect of our rendering satisfaction to the justice of God by our own works, but because we are judged of in connection with Christ’s righteousness, which we have put on by faith, that it might become ours. On this account I have preferred to retain the particle ἐν, (in,) rather than substitute in its place per, (through,) for that signification corresponds better with Paul’s intention.
The force of the preposition ἐν (in,) as made use of by the Apostle in this passage, is more fully brought out by Beza in the following terms: “Justi apud Deum, et quidem justitia non nobis inh’rente, sed qu’, quum in Christo sit, nobis per fidem a Deo imputatur. Ideo enim additurn est: ἐν αὐτῷ Sic ergo sumus justitia Dei in ipso, ut ille est peccatum in nobis, nempe ex imputatione. Libet autem hic ex Augustino locum insignem exscribere, velut istius commentarium plenissimum. Sic igitur ille Serm. 5. de verbis Apostoli: Deus Pater eum, qui non noverat peccatum (nempe Iesum Christum) peccatum effecit,ut nos simus justitia Dei (non nostra) in ipso (non in nobis.) His adde Philippians 3:9;” — “Righteous before God, and that by a righteousness which is not inherent in us, but which, being in Christ, is imputed to us by God through faith. For it is on this account that it is added: ἐν αὐτῷ (in him.) We are, therefore, the righteousness of God in him in the same way as he is sin in us — by imputation. I may here quote a remarkable passage from Augustine, as a most complete commentary upon it. In Serm. 5 on the words of the Apostle he expresses himself thus: God the Father made him sin who had not known sin, (Jesus Christ,) that we might be the righteousness of God (not our own) in him (not in ourselves.) To these add Philippians 3:9.” — Ed.
CHAPTER 6
2 Corinthians 6:1-10
1. We then, as workers together with him, beseech you also that ye receive not the grace of God in vain.
1. Nos vero adiuvantes (vel, collaborantes)
“Ainsi done en ouurant auec luy, ou, estans ses ouuriers;” — “Thus then in working with him, or, being his workmen.”
etiam obsecramus, ne frustra gratiam Dei receperitis.
2. (For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)
2. Dicit enim (Ies. 49, 8) Tempore accepto exaudivi te, et in die salutis auxiliatus sum tibi: ecce, nunc tempus acceptum: ecce, nunc dies salutis.
3. Giving no offence in any thing, that the ministry be not blamed:
3. Nullum dantes
“Ne donnans aucun scandale, ou, donnons;” — “Giving no offense, or, we give.”
ulla in re offensionem, ut ne vituperetur ministerium:
4. But in all things approving ourselves as the ministers of God, in much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses,
4. Sed in omnibus commendantes nos
“Mais nous rendans louables en toutes choses, ou, Mais rendons nous louables;” — “But rendering ourselves approvable in all things, or, We render ourselves approvable.”
tanquam Dei mœrore, in patientia multa, in afflictionibus, in necessitatibus, in angustiis,
5. In stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings;
5. In plagis, in carceribus, in seditionibus, in laboribus, in vigiliis, in ieiuniis;
6. By pureness, by knowledge, by longsuffering, by kindness, by the Holy Ghost, by love unfeigned,
6. In sinceritate, in scientia, in tolerantia, in mansuetudine, in Spiritu Sancto, in caritate non ficta,
7. By the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left,
7. In sermone veritatis, in potentia Dei, per arma iustitiæ dextra et sinistra:
8. By honour and dishonour, by evil report and good report: as deceivers, and yet true;
8. Per gloriam et ignominiam, per infamiam, et bonam famam: tanquam impostores, tamen veraces:
9. As unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and, behold, we live; as chastened, and not killed;
9. Tanquam ignoti, tamen celebres: tanquam morientes, et ecce, vivimus; tanquam castigati, tamen morte non affecti:
10. As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.

               <ns0:p n="1">1 FOr we know, that if <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.7. 2 Pet. 1.13, 14.</ns0:note> our earthly house of <ns0:hi>this</ns0:hi> tabernable were dissolved <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle had before said, that he looked at the things not seen; in this verse he openeth himself, and sheweth what those unseen things are: <ns0:hi>We</ns0:hi> (saith he) <ns0:hi>know,</ns0:hi> we have a cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain perswasion, we doubt not of it<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but that if our body were dissolved. This body he calleth an <ns0:hi>Earthly house,</ns0:hi> either because it is made of the dust of the earth, into which it must again be resolved; or because it is only the habitation of the Soul, so long as the Soul is on this side of Heaven; and therefore he cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />leth it also, the <ns0:hi>Earthly house</ns0:hi> of this <ns0:hi>Tabernacle.</ns0:hi> A Tabernacle is a moving House or Booth builded up for a time; This Taber<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nacle (saith the Apostle) must be pulled down, and taken in pieces; and we are certain, that if it be dissolved,</ns0:note>, we have a building of God <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">we have a <ns0:hi>building of God,</ns0:hi> either a blessed, eternal Mansion, (accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to that of our Saviour, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 14.2. <ns0:hi>In my Fathers house there are many mansions</ns0:hi>) or else, God will give us a spiritual, glorious, incorruptible Body.</ns0:note>, an house not made with hands <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not an House made with hands, nor an House that shall be dissolved and any more pulled down, but which shall be</ns0:note>, eternal in the heavens <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Eternal in the Heavens</ns0:hi>; in such a state, as that it shall be incorruptible, and no more subject to any cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ruption or decay.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 For in this <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 8.23.</ns0:note> we groan earnestly, desiring to be clothed upon with our house, which is from heaven <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">We are so confident of such a blessed state, that we passio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nately desire to be invested into it. And this <ns0:hi>Groaning</ns0:hi> is also an Evidence of it, for the desire of Grace shall not be made frustrated. It is against the Nature of man to desire death, which is the stripping or unclothing the Soul of flesh; but not to desire that the garment of immortality may be put upon mortality, (which is that our house from Heaven, which is mentioned in <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 If so be that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rev. 3.18.</ns0:note> being clothed, we shall not be found naked <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Some make the <ns0:hi>Clothing</ns0:hi> here spoken of, different from the <ns0:hi>Clothing</ns0:hi> before mentioned. And make this Verse restrictive of what the Apostle had before said, of the certainty which some have of being clothed upon with a glorious Body. <ns0:hi>If so be</ns0:hi> (saith the Apostle) <ns0:hi>we be not found naked,</ns0:hi> but clothed, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> with the Wedding-garment of Christs Righteousness; for con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning those that do not die in the Lord, that do not watch, and keep their garments, it is said <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 16.15. <ns0:hi>They shall walk naked,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>men shall se<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                        </ns0:gap> their shame.</ns0:hi> But considering the cloth<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing before mentioned, was not this clothing, but the superin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ducing of an immortal, incorruptible, glorious state of body, upon our mortal, corruptible state; some judicious Interpre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters think, that the clothing here mentioned, is the clothing of the Soul with the Body. It is manifest, that the Apostles ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prehended Christs second Coming much nearer than it hath proved. Therefore he saith, 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 4.15. <ns0:hi>We that are alive</ns0:hi> (supposing that generation might live) to Christs <ns0:hi>second Coming:</ns0:hi> and 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.51. <ns0:hi>We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be chan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLunhyphen" />ged.</ns0:hi> This some think (and that not improbably) is the cause of this passage; the sense of which they judge to be this: If so be that we be, at the Resurrection, found in the flesh, clothed still with our bodies, and shall not be found <ns0:hi>naked,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>stript of our flesh,</ns0:hi> and dead before that time.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 For we that are in <ns0:hi>this</ns0:hi> tabernacle, do groan, being burdened <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Tabernacle</ns0:hi> he meaneth (as he had before expounded it) the earthly house of our body. <ns0:hi>Do groan,</ns0:hi> both with a groaning of grief, and also <ns0:hi>of desire. Being burd<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ned,</ns0:hi> either with the <ns0:hi>body of flesh</ns0:hi>; or with <ns0:hi>Sin</ns0:hi> (the body of death) <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.24. or with the load of <ns0:hi>Trials</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Afflictions.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, not for that we would be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clothed <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Not that we would be unclothed,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>die,</ns0:hi> be unclothed of our flesh, (Nature abhorreth death, and flyeth from it) but <ns0:hi>clothed upon</ns0:hi>; which is expounded 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.53. <ns0:hi>Our corruptible having put on incor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ruption, and our mortal having put on immortality.</ns0:hi> And this con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firmeth what was observed before, that the Apostles had some perswasion, (<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hough not from any Divine Revelation of that hour) that the Resurrection, and Day of Judgment, would be before the determination of that Age and Generation; that so we might come into the possessions of Eternal Life, (for that the Apostle meaneth by <ns0:hi>mortality being swallowed up of life.</ns0:hi>) Death is not desirable for its own sake, but upon the account of that immortal life, Into which it leadeth the Souls of Belie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers; nor (as was said before) doth the Apostle here directly desire death, (which is that which in this Verse he calleth <ns0:hi>un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clothing</ns0:hi>) but rather the <ns0:hi>change</ns0:hi> mentioned 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.52. which he here calleth a <ns0:hi>clothing upon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life <ns0:hi>i.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Now <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 29.23. Eph. 2.10.</ns0:note> he that hath wrought us for the self same thing <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> God <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>self same thing</ns0:hi> is <ns0:hi>the life,</ns0:hi> the Eternal life, mentioned in the former Verse; <ns0:hi>the house in the Heavens, not made with hands, v.</ns0:hi> 2. God hath <ns0:hi>wrought</ns0:hi> us for it, (as some interpret the Text) in Creation, and by his Providence, forming our bodies in the womb: but it is much better interpreted by others concerning <ns0:hi>Regeneration</ns0:hi>; for in the first birth (without respect to the De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cree of Election) God hath no more wrought us for it, than the worst of men. The Apostle therefore is, doubtless, to be understood, as speaking concerning the <ns0:hi>work of Grace,</ns0:hi> which is here attributed to God; we have not wrought our selves in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to, or up to any fitness or any grounded expectation of the fu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture blessed and glorious estate; but it is God who hath prepa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red us for it, and wrought such a lively hope of it in us.</ns0:note>, who hath also given unto us the earnest of the Spirit <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">And hath also <ns0:hi>given us his holy Spirit</ns0:hi> as the Pledge and <ns0:hi>Earnest</ns0:hi> of it: (Concerning this, see 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.21.) he hath given us his Spirit to dwell and to work in us, and to assure us of what we speak of, <ns0:hi>viz. The house in the Heavens, the building of God, that is not made with hands.</ns0:hi> The Spirit of Grace given to the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple of God, working and dwelling in them, is a certain pledge of that Glory and Life Eternal, which he hath prepared for them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 Therefore <ns0:hi>we are</ns0:hi> always confident, knowing that whilst we are at home in the body, we are ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent from the Lord <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">We are always full of courage and comfort, being confident of this Glory, and the <ns0:hi>swallowing up of mortality in life:</ns0:hi> For we know, that while we are in our earthly home, (which is our body) we are furthest off from that which is our true home (which is Heaven) from the vision and fruition of God; for Believers are but <ns0:hi>strangers</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>pilgrims on the earth, desiring a better coun<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ry, that is an heavenly,</ns0:hi> Heb. 11.16.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 8.23, 24. 1 Cor. 13.12.</ns0:note> we walk by faith, not by sight <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">That is, we live, and order our conversations, not by <ns0:hi>sight,</ns0:hi> or any <ns0:hi>evidence of sense,</ns0:hi> but by <ns0:hi>Faith,</ns0:hi> (which is described by the Apostle, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11.1. to be <ns0:hi>the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.</ns0:hi>) We see nothing here by the eye of sense but mortality, corruption, and misery; but by Faith we see another more excellent and glorious state, and we order our life according to our Faith, and fight of things that are in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />visible: Or <ns0:hi>Sight</ns0:hi> here may be taken more strictly for the bea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tifick Vision prepared in Heaven for the Sa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>s.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 We are confident, <ns0:hi>I say,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Phil. 1.23.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>illing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">We are confident of such a blessed state, and this makes us willing to be out of this body, that we might have the glorious presence and injoyment of God to all Eternity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 Wherefore we <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>we endea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vour.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> labour, that whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Having such an hope, yea not such an hope only, but such an assurance and confidence, we <ns0:hi>labour,</ns0:hi> both Actively, doing the Will of God, and Passively, submitting to the Will of God in all afflictive Providences; that while we are in the body, and ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent from the Lord, we may be <ns0:hi>accepted</ns0:hi> of him; as we know we shall be, when we shall be present with him, in another sense than we now are.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 14.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The Apostle declareth, either the ground of his confi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence, or (rather) the reason of his, and other Believers la<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bour, so to behave themselves, as that, both in life and death, they might be accepted of God; that was, his knowledge and firm belief of the last Judgment. It is called the <ns0:hi>Iudgment-seat of Christ,</ns0:hi> because he it is whom God hath appointed to be the <ns0:hi>Iudge both of the quick, and the dead,</ns0:hi> Acts 10.42. The word translated <ns0:hi>Appear,</ns0:hi> is <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which signifieth to be made manifest, and so signifieth not only to appear, but to be inqui<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red into, searched, and examined, and narrowly fi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ted; And this lets us know, that those Texts which speak of Believers not being judged, or not coming into Judgment, must not be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood of the <ns0:hi>Iudgment</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Inquiry</ns0:hi>; (for all shall come into that Judgment) but of the <ns0:hi>Iudgment</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Condemnation.</ns0:hi> And i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> lets us also know the vanity of their Opinion, who think that <ns0:hi>Pagans</ns0:hi> shall not rise again in the last Day.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 2.6. Gal. 6.7. Eph. 6.8. Col. 3.24, 2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Rev. 22.12<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> that every one may receive the things <ns0:hi>done</ns0:hi> in his body, according to that he hath done, whether <ns0:hi>it be</ns0:hi> good or bad <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The End of this Judgment is declared, that <ns0:hi>Every man may receive according to what he hath done in his body</ns0:hi>; that is, according to the thoughts he hath thought, the words that he hath spoken, the actions which he hath done, during the time that his Soul dwelt upon the Earth in his body; whether the things which he did in that state were good, and such things as God required; or sinful, and contrary to the revealed Will of God. What this <ns0:hi>Receiving</ns0:hi> means, we are told <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 25.46. <ns0:hi>These shall go away into everlasting punishment,</ns0:hi> but the <ns0:hi>Righteous into life eternal.</ns0:hi> Hence we read <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.29. of a <ns0:hi>Resurrection of life,</ns0:hi> and a <ns0:hi>Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />surrection of damnation.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:464" />11 Knowing therefore the <ns0:note place="margin">Job 31.23. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>de 23.</ns0:note> terror of the Lord, we perswade men <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">We believing and being fully perswaded, that there shall be such a great and terrible day of the Lord, when there shall be such a narrow inquiry and search into whatsoever men have thought, spoke, or done in the flesh; <ns0:hi>we perswade men</ns0:hi> to be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve in the Lord Jesus Christ, to walk according to the Rule of the Gospel, to be charitable towards us, and not to censure, or judge us, or use against us hard speeches.</ns0:note>; but <ns0:note place="margin">Chap. 4.2.</ns0:note> we are made manifest unto God, and I trust also, are made manifest in your consciences <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">If any will not be perswaded to think well of us, yet the sincerity of our hearts and ways is made manifest unto God; he knoweth what we are, and how we have behaved our selves: And I trust we have so behaved our selves, that we are not only made manifest unto God, but we are manifest unto your Consciences; so as your Consciences will bear us a testimony, how we have beha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved our selves amongst you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 For we <ns0:note place="margin">Chap 3.1.</ns0:note> commend not our selves again unto you <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">I do not speak this to commend my self unto you; he had before declared, that he trusted that he was made manifest to their Consciences, and so needed not further to commend him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self. But (saith he)</ns0:note>, but give you occasion to <ns0:note place="margin">Chap. 1.14.</ns0:note> glory on our be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />half, that you may have somewhat to <ns0:hi>answer</ns0:hi> them which glory <ns0:note place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>in the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> in appearance, and not in heart <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">I speak it only to give you <ns0:hi>occasion to glory,</ns0:hi> to glory in me as the Apostle of Christ unto you, or to defend me against the scandals and reproaches of those that re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proach me, when themselves have no true inward cause of glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rying, though they have in outward appearance, in respect of their riches, wit, wisdom, or the like.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 For <ns0:note place="margin">Chap. 11.1, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 17. & 12. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> whether we be besides our selves, <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> to God <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">It should seem, that some amongst the <ns0:hi>Corinthians,</ns0:hi> a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst other reproaches, had reproaches <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> for a <ns0:hi>mad man</ns0:hi>; either taking advantage of the <ns0:hi>warmth</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>fervour of his Spirit,</ns0:hi> or of those <ns0:hi>Ecstasies</ns0:hi> in which he sometimes was; or of his speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing things which they could not apprehend and understand: as the <ns0:hi>Roman Governour,</ns0:hi> in the <ns0:hi>Acts,</ns0:hi> told him, <ns0:hi>Much learning had made him mad.</ns0:hi> The Apostle tells them, That if indeed he was besides himself in any of their opinion, it was <ns0:hi>unto God,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>for the honour</ns0:hi> and glory of God.</ns0:note>: or whether we be sober, <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> for your cause <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Or if he was sober, it was <ns0:hi>for their sake</ns0:hi>; in what temper soever he was, it was either for service to God, or them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 For the love of Christ constraineth us <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Love of Christ</ns0:hi> signifieth either that love towards the Son<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of men which was in Christ before the Foundation of the World; for even then (as <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> telleth us) <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 8.31. he was <ns0:hi>Rejoycing in the habitable parts of the earth, and his delight was with the sons of men</ns0:hi>: which Love shewed it self in time, in his coming and assuming our Natures, and dying upon the Cross for us; <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 15.13. <ns0:hi>Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.</ns0:hi> Or else it signifieth that <ns0:hi>habit of Love</ns0:hi> to Christ, which is in every Believer; for it is true of either of these, that they <ns0:hi>constrain</ns0:hi> a Believers Soul.</ns0:note>, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause we thus judge <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Because (saith the Apostle) we thus account, or reason, That <ns0:hi>if one died for all—All</ns0:hi> here is interpreted according to the various notions of men, about the extent of the Death of Christ. Some by the term understanding <ns0:hi>all individuals</ns0:hi>; some, all the <ns0:hi>Elect,</ns0:hi> or all those that should believe in Christ; others, some of all Nations, Jews or Gentiles. Be it as it will, that point is not to be determined by this Universal Particle, which is as often in Scripture used in a restrained sense, as in a more general sense.</ns0:note>: that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 3.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> if one died for all, then were all dead <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Apostle here concludeth, That if one <ns0:hi>died for all, then all were dead</ns0:hi>; which is to be understood of a spiritual death, as <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.1. And the Apostles Argument dependeth upon this, That if all, for whom Christ died, had not been dead in sin, there then had been no need of his dying for to expiate their sin, and to redeem them from the guilt and power of it; but be they what they would, for whom Christ died, whether all Individuals, or all the Elect only, his dying for them was a ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifest Evidence that they were dead.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> he died for all, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 16.11, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 20. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 3.10. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 4.2.</ns0:note> that they which live, should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">And he died for all those for whom he died, not only to redeem them from the guilt of sin, but also from their <ns0:hi>vain con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versation</ns0:hi>; that they which live by his Grace, might not make themselves the end of their life, and live to serve themselves, and gratifie their own corrupt inclinations; but might make the service of Christ, the honour and glory of him who died for them, and also rose again from the dead, the end of their lives; arguing the reasonableness of an holy and Christian life, from the Love and End of Christ in dying for them; according to that, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 14.7, 8. <ns0:hi>For none of us liveth to himself, and no man dieth to himself; for whether we live, we live unto the Lord, and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether therefore we live, or die, we are the Lords.</ns0:hi> This is one way by which a Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liever fetcheth strength from the Death of Christ to die unto sin, and from his Resurrection to live unto newness of life; he con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cluding, If Christ died, and rose again for him, that then he was once dead in trespasses and sins; and therefore he judgeth himself obliged, now that he is made spiritually alive, not to live to himself, to serve his own profit, honour, reputation, lusts, or passions, but to live in obedience to him, and to the honour and glory of him who died to redeem him from the guilt and power of sin, and rose again to quicken him to new<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of life and conversation, to the honour and glory of his Redeemer.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matt. 12.50. Joh. 15.14. Gal. 5.6.</ns0:note> Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Words of sense in Scripture ordinarily signifie more than the act of that sense which they express; particularly this term <ns0:hi>Know,</ns0:hi> ordinarily signifieth to <ns0:hi>approve</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>acknowledge</ns0:hi>; and so it signifies here. We <ns0:hi>know,</ns0:hi> that is, we regard, we acknow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge no man in the discharge of our Office; we regard no man, with respect to any external fleshly consideration. Under which notion he comprehends all things not spiritual, whether carnal relations, riches, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>; yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> no more <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Nay, though we have known Christ after the flesh</ns0:hi>; not from any sight of him (for we read not that <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> at any time saw Christ) but <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 9. when he saw him, not according to the flesh, but as exalted at the right hand of God: but by the hearing of the ear <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> had known Christ, as one that had lived in the flesh, and who had conversed with men for above thirty years; Yet (saith he) we know him no more, we shall neither see, nor hear him any more in the flesh; we now only know him as he hath a <ns0:hi>glorious Body</ns0:hi>; with which he sitteth at the right hand of God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 Therefore if any man <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 8.9.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> in Christ, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>let him be.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>he is</ns0:hi> a new creature: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 43.18, 19. & 65.17. Rev. 21.5.</ns0:note> old things are passed away, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold, all things are become new <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>If any man be in Christ,</ns0:hi> is as much as, if any man be im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />planted, or ingrafted into Christ, by Faith united to him, he is a <ns0:hi>new Creature</ns0:hi> [the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> is, a <ns0:hi>new creation.</ns0:hi>] A Phrase, which argueth the greatest change imaginable, and such a one as can be wrought in the Soul by no other power, than the Pow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er of God. We have the same expression <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.15. The <ns0:hi>Ellipsis</ns0:hi> of the Verb make some translate it [<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>] <ns0:hi>him be a new Creature,</ns0:hi> supplying <ns0:gap reason="foreign">

                     </ns0:gap> for <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. But the next words shew us, that the Apostle is speaking of what is past, <ns0:hi>Old things are passed away,</ns0:hi> old Affections, Passions, Notions, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> He hath the same Soul, but new qualities, new apprehensions in his Understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, new inclinations in his Will and Affections, new thoughts, counsels, and designs. The <ns0:hi>Predicate</ns0:hi> sheweth that the term, <ns0:hi>be in christ,</ns0:hi> cannot be understood of those that are only in the Church, and turned from <ns0:hi>Paganism</ns0:hi> to the <ns0:hi>Christian Faith</ns0:hi>; (for there are many such in the World, in whom there is no new Creation, and who have in them nothing of this new Creature)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 And all things <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> of God <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This Change, which is wrought in our Hearts, is not of our selves, but wrought in us by the great and mighty Power of God: so <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1.13. <ns0:hi>Which were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God</ns0:hi>; Of God, as the principal efficient Cause.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Col. 1.20. 1 Joh. 2.2. & 4.10.</ns0:note> who hath re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />conciled us unto himself by Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Who, by the Blood of his Son Jesus Christ, <ns0:hi>meritoriously,</ns0:hi> and by the Spirit of Christ, <ns0:hi>actually,</ns0:hi> hath reconciled us unto himself; of Enemies hath made us Friends.</ns0:note>, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>And hath given us the Ministry of Reconciliation,</ns0:hi> hath betrust<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed us with the preaching of the Gospel: It is God that hath re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />conciled us; it is Christ by whom we are reconciled, his Blood is the Price of our Reconciliation: But he committed to his Apostles, and so to the successive Ministers of the Gospel, the <ns0:hi>Ministry of Reconciliation,</ns0:hi> that is, the Ministry of the Gospel, by which this Reconciliation is published to such as are as yet Ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies to God. They have but a <ns0:hi>Ministration</ns0:hi> in it; God hath appointed them to publish and to declare it and to intreat men to be reconciled unto him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 To wit, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 3.24, 25.</ns0:note> that God was in Christ, reconci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling the world to himself <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>world</ns0:hi> here, some would understand <ns0:hi>all Mankind,</ns0:hi> and by <ns0:hi>Reconciling</ns0:hi> no more than making God <ns0:hi>reconcileable</ns0:hi>; but this proceedeth from an over-fondness of their Principle of <ns0:hi>Christs dying for all, and every man.</ns0:hi> For as it is manifest from a mul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />titude of Scriptures, that <ns0:hi>World</ns0:hi> is many times taken in a much more limited and restrained sense; so there is nothing here that guides us to interpret it in such a latitude: nay, that which fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />loweth, doth manifestly so restrain it; for <ns0:hi>God was not in Christ<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> reconciling the world to himself,</ns0:hi> that is, every man and woman in the World, so <ns0:hi>as not to impute their sins</ns0:hi> to them.</ns0:note>, not imputing their trespasses unto them <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This the Apostle here affirmeth; which makes it manifest, that by <ns0:hi>World</ns0:hi> here is meant many, some of all sorts, as well Gentiles as Jews; even so many as he pleaseth not to impute their sins unto.</ns0:note>, and hath <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>put in us.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> committed unto us the word of reconciliation <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Now (saith the Apostle) the dispensing and publishing that Word, by which this Reconciliation is made known to the Children of men, God hath committed to us; to us, that are Apostles, and so to the Ministers of the Gospel, that shall succeed us in the Work of the Ministry. This mightily commendeth the Gospel, and the preaching of it, that it is the Word by which, as a means, Souls are reconciled unto God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:465" />20 Now then we are <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 33.23. Mal. 2.7. Chap. 3.6.</ns0:note> ambassadours for Christ, as though God did beseech <ns0:hi>you</ns0:hi> by us: we pray you in Christs stead, Be ye reconciled to God <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The Apostle here giveth us a true Notion, not only of A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postles, which were the first and principal Ministers of the Gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel, but of all other Ministers; teaching us what all Ministers should be, and what all true Ministers of the Gospel are. They <ns0:hi>are Ambassadours for Christ</ns0:hi>; there is by Nature an enmity be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />twixt the Creature and God; he naturally hateth God, and God is angry with him. Those <ns0:hi>that were sometimes alienated, and Enemies in their minds by wicked works,</ns0:hi> Christ <ns0:hi>hath reconciled in the body of his flesh through death,.</ns0:hi> Col. 1.21, 22. He hath purchased a <ns0:hi>reconciliation</ns0:hi> for them. But yet, till they have re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceived Christ, as their Lord and Saviour, they are not actually recovered to God by him. God does by men, as great <ns0:hi>Princes</ns0:hi> do by such as they are at Enmity with; he sends his Ministers to them, who are his Ambassadours; and as all Ambassadours re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />present the Person of him whose Ambassadours they are, and speak in his name, and as in his stead, perswading to peace; so these speak as in Christ's name, and in God's stead; their business is <ns0:hi>to beseech men</ns0:hi> to be reconciled unto God, to lay down their Arms, and to accept of the terms of the Gospel for peace and reconciliation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gal. 3.13. 1 Joh. 3.5.</ns0:note> he hath made him <ns0:hi>to be</ns0:hi> sin for us, who knew no sin <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Christ knew no sin, as he was guilty of no sin; <ns0:hi>which of you</ns0:hi> (saith he <ns0:hi>Iob.</ns0:hi> 8.46.) <ns0:hi>convinceth me of sin?</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.21, 22, 24. <ns0:hi>He did no sin, nor was guil<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> sound in his mouth.</ns0:hi> But God made him <ns0:hi>to be sin for us; He was numbred amongst the transgres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sours,</ns0:hi> Isai. 53.6, 12. Our sins were reckoned to him; so as though personally he was no Sinner, yet by imputation he was, and God dealt with him as such; Or he was made a Sacrifice for our sins, a <ns0:hi>Sin-offering</ns0:hi>; so answering the Type in the Law, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 4.3.25.29. & 5, 6. & 7.2.</ns0:note>, that we might be made the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 1.17.</ns0:note> righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness of God in him <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">that so his <ns0:hi>righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness</ns0:hi> might be imputed to us, and we might be made righteous with such a righteousness as those souls must have whom God will accept. As Christ was not made sin by any sin inherent in him, so neither are we made righteous by any righteousness in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />herent in us, but by the righteousness of Christ imputed to us; as he was a Sinner by the sins of his people reckoned and im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />puted unto him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
